tells.1: The 'third plate of the night' feels like manufactured kitchen specificity: the third plate hardly tests consistency under pressure.
tells.2: The tidy trio of scheduling benefits adds a sweeping promise—'a schedule you can plan a life around'—that the stated opening hours don't establish.
tells.4: The bold template headings and polished recruitment phrases make the voice feel more packaged than personal.

reason: Version 1 has the best balance of voice, concrete responsibilities and readable prose, although its scheduling promises need verification. Version 3 feels plausibly human but ranks last as skilled writing for this purpose because it is repetitive, vague and unnecessarily discouraging; stylistic tells don't establish authorship.
